verdict.worst_problem: Enrichment and GSEA are run on pseudo-replicate Wilcoxon rankings that may still be depth-driven, since the depth-matched results are not used to filter the gene lists fed into pathway analysis.
The pathway enrichment steps (ORA and GSEA) use the original DE results from Step 3 rather than the depth-matched DE results from Step 5, risking the enrichment of depth-driven technical artifacts.
Composition analysis is uninformative with one library per condition (sample_key = condition_key), so proportion shifts and the >20% loss flag remain uncalibrated heuristics.
Running both ORA and GSEA on the same descriptive rankings is slightly redundant and may overcomplicate the interpretation of an already exploratory analysis.

It misreads the design as one library per condition when orig.ident has a single level (both arms multiplexed in one library), and spends effort on de novo clustering/resolution selection and a conditional re-annotation rule when 11 curated majorclass labels are already available and used downstream anyway.
Re-clustering and re-annotating the cells (Steps 3 and 4) is largely unnecessary busywork when high-quality `majorclass` and `celltype` annotations already exist in the dataset.
Re-clustering and doublet removal largely duplicate the existing majorclass/celltype annotations, adding steps that are not used downstream while DE still relies on the provided labels.
Re-clustering the data is unnecessary busywork since the dataset already provides high-resolution 'majorclass' and 'celltype' annotations.

Both ORA and GSEA plus a cross-class synthesis add redundant downstream layers on rankings that are explicitly non-inferential, and the depth-matched results are never used to filter the pathway inputs.
Running both ORA (Step 6) and GSEA (Step 7) on the same descriptive rankings is slightly redundant, though acceptable for exploratory analysis.

With one library per arm and no replicates, even depth-matched Wilcoxon rankings and downstream enrichment/GSEA remain confounded by batch, so pathway-level claims (steps 5-6) risk over-interpretation despite the descriptive framing.
Step 3 uses orig.ident as sample_key, but since it has only 1 level across all cells, it cannot separate the two conditions for composition analysis.

Redundant/overbuilt enrichment layers (ORA plus GSEA on both directions of 11 classes) and a marker-validation step with an arbitrary 80% concordance rule add busywork without changing conclusions, and step 2's DE is described as within-sample when it is not.
Running both ORA and GSEA on descriptive DE results derived from unreplicated samples risks over-interpreting technical noise as coordinated biological pathways.
Step 2's de-novo clustering/UMAP is largely redundant busywork given annotations already exist, and both ORA and GSEA are run on the same lists adding little beyond each other.
Running de novo clustering is slightly inefficient if the UMAP is purely intended as a visualization scaffold for existing annotations.
Minor gene-marker errors (OPN4 assigned to cones, ARRB3 for rods) and the fact that both arms sit in one library means arm-specific batch/ambient effects remain unaddressable beyond depth matching.
None; the plan is exceptionally well-designed, perfectly tailored to the dataset's specific constraints, and rigorously addresses both the depth confound and the lack of biological replicates.

ORA/GSEA steps still rely on pseudoreplicated p-value thresholds the plan itself declares invalid, and the annotation-concordance check plus both enrichment approaches add limited value relative to their cost.

ORA relies on an adjusted p-value threshold (p < 0.05) which will be massively inflated due to pseudoreplication, potentially feeding an overly broad list of genes into the enrichment test despite the descriptive caveat.

It assumes tool-specific outputs and columns (e.g., scANVI_prediction_max_probability, min_cells guards, per-arm cell counts implying which classes are skipped) that aren't confirmed in the stated obs metadata, and composition with n=1 per arm remains uninterpretable beyond description.
Running both ORA and GSEA on descriptive, pseudoreplicated rankings is slightly redundant, though the plan explicitly justifies the complementary approach.

Some details are wrong or sloppy (e.g., OPN4 cited as a cone marker, min_cells=30 claimed to exclude six classes without checking actual counts, and a 3% mito cut plus HVG re-clustering that adds little given labels are reused).
No significant problems identified; the plan is exceptionally rigorous and perfectly addresses the dataset's specific limitations (n=1 and depth imbalance).

Some assumptions are asserted rather than verified (e.g., scANVI probability columns are presumed present, and the claim that depth inflation can only manufacture up-regulation is oversimplified), and ORA+GSEA on pseudoreplicated rankings adds redundancy.
No significant problems; this is an exceptionally rigorous, dataset-aware, and statistically sound analysis plan.

Some steps are partially redundant or over-engineered (ORA plus GSEA plus Jaccard lens-scoring plus a decision-tree classifier) and the marker-validation '80% concordance' and curated-gene-list criteria are underspecified, risking arbitrary interpretive calls.
The plan proposes analyzing microglial activation signatures in steps 8 and 10 despite explicitly skipping the Microglia majorclass in step 3 due to insufficient cell counts.

Step 3's canonical marker list is copy-pasted nonsense (SLC1A3/NEFL assigned to nearly every class), so annotation validation as written cannot work; also step 7 filters on p-values the plan itself declares invalid.
Step 3 lists the exact same canonical markers (SLC1A3/NEFL) for ten completely different cell types, which is biologically invalid and indicates a copy-paste error in the marker dictionary.

Step 3's annotation audit assumes scANVI probability columns and cites shaky markers (SLC1A3/NEFL for Rod) that aren't listed in the dataset's obs, and some checks (housekeeping panel, ORA+GSEA+synthesis) overlap in what they establish.

Using ribosomal protein genes as housekeeping controls in single-nucleus RNA-seq (Step 10) is unreliable because they are predominantly cytoplasmic and often depleted or highly variable in nuclear preparations.
Some marker-gene expectations in the validation step are wrong/garbled (e.g., OPN1MW for rods, SLC1A3/SLC6A6 for bipolar cells, 'SYNX2' for amacrine), which could cause spurious label downgrades.

No major problems identified; the plan is exceptionally rigorous, perfectly tailored to the dataset's constraints, and explicitly handles both the depth confound and the lack of biological replicates.
Minor inaccuracies (e.g., SLC17A7 cited as an amacrine marker, snRNA-seq inference) and some overlap between ORA/GSEA/synthesis steps, but the core design is sound.
None.
Some marker assertions are wrong/copy-pasted (SLC1A3/NEFL listed for both BC and AC), and the claimed minor-class cell-count exclusions are asserted rather than verified from the data.
None.
Some marker-panel choices are wrong/garbled (e.g., OPN4/NEUROD1 for cones, SOX2 for RGC, duplicated MG panel) and steps 9-10 overlap substantially with the depth-matching output, adding redundancy.
Running ORA and GSEA on pseudoreplicated, n=1 differential expression rankings risks generating highly significant but biologically spurious pathway narratives, despite the exploratory caveats.

Some steps are busywork or wrong-headed (doublet re-detection on already all-Singlet data, mitochondrial filtering on nuclei, and step 5's marker expectations list misassigns markers, e.g. SLC1A3/SLC1A4 for BC/AC/Cone).
The expected marker genes listed in Step 5 are biologically inaccurate for several retinal cell types (e.g., SLC1A3/SLC1A4 are glial markers, not markers for Amacrine cells or Cones).

Some steps are over-engineered or shaky in detail (e.g., miscited canonical markers like SLC1A3 for bipolar cells and OPN4/NEUROD1 for cones, plus overlapping synthesis/interpretation steps), which could mislead the annotation concordance check.

The plan incorrectly assumes that a single `orig.ident` implies one library per arm with collinear batch effects, whereas a single `orig.ident` across two conditions actually indicates the samples were multiplexed into the exact same library, eliminating the technical batch confound.

Steps 12 and to a lesser extent 3–4 add speculative custom scoring/lens-comparison and re-clustering busywork whose ad hoc gene sets and concordance heuristics could over-interpret an n=1 descriptive contrast.
No major problems; the plan is exceptionally well-tailored to the dataset's specific constraints and technical nuances.
The annotation-concordance step uses fabricated placeholder marker symbols (SAG2–SAG11) instead of real retinal lineage markers, so that validation step as written cannot run meaningfully.
Despite extensive caveats, computing adjusted p-values on unreplicated data (Step 5) risks misinterpretation by downstream consumers who may ignore the warnings.

The report never considers that the uniform pan-cell-type upregulation of ribosomal/translation and mitochondrial genes is a classic sequencing-depth/normalisation artefact, and instead interprets it as a unified biological stress program.

The report interprets the pan-retinal upregulation of ribosomal and translation genes as a biological stress response, failing to recognize it is likely a technical artefact caused by the DDX41 library being sequenced much more deeply than the WT library.

The report never considers that the identical pan-cell-type upregulation of ribosomal/translation genes is most likely a sequencing-depth/normalisation artefact, and instead interprets it as a biological pan-retinal stress response.

The report interprets a pan-retinal upregulation of translation genes as a biological stress response without considering it might be a technical artefact driven by differences in sequencing depth between the two single libraries.

The abstract and discussion assert causal, 'significant' biological reorganization (including the pan-cell-type translation/ribosome up-shift) without the depth-confound and no-replication caveats that the limitations section correctly states.

Uses the word 'significant' colloquially to describe proportional shifts ('significant reorganization') despite explicitly noting that no valid statistical tests for proportion shifts could be performed.

The pan-cell-type ribosomal/translation upregulation is almost certainly the 1.6x per-cell sequencing-depth difference, yet the report interprets it biologically as a 'compensatory translational surge' and mislabels the depth confound in Limitation 5 as a mere difference in cell numbers.

The report fails to identify the data as single-nucleus RNA-seq despite the low mitochondrial content and nuclear_fraction column, inappropriately applying a 10% mitochondrial threshold instead of a stricter 1-5% threshold suitable for nuclei.

It never considers that the pan-cell-type translation/ribosomal up-shift (and the higher genes-per-cell in the DDX41 arm) could be a sequencing-depth/normalisation artefact, instead interpreting it as coordinated biology, while still leaning on FDR=0.0/padj<0.05-based pathway calls it elsewhere disclaims.

Fails to recognize that a pan-cell-type upregulation of ribosomal/translation genes coupled with higher gene detection in the mutant arm is highly likely to be a sequencing depth or normalization artefact rather than biology.

The report never considers that the pan-cell-type, same-direction up-regulation of ribosomal/translation genes (and the higher genes-per-cell in the DDX41 arm, which it instead interprets as biology) is most likely a sequencing-depth/normalisation artefact.

The report interprets the pan-retinal upregulation of ribosomal and translation genes as a biological 'global translational activation', failing to recognize it as a classic technical artifact caused by the DDX41 library being sequenced much more deeply than the WT library.

Despite good caveating, the report reports FDR<0.05 'significant' term counts as findings and its stratified per-class cell counts (e.g. AC 469 WT/181 DDX41, Rod 6,578/3,479) contradict the dataset table (AC 258/392, Rod 5,973/4,084), indicating unsupported/garbled numbers.

The report fails to identify the data as single-nucleus RNA-seq despite the nuclear_fraction column, missing the need for a stricter mitochondrial threshold, and briefly lapses into reporting 'significant' GSEA terms based on FDR despite acknowledging the lack of biological replicates.

Despite good caveats, the report still treats FDR-based GSEA counts and 'FDR = 0.0' NES values as findings and downplays the 1.6x depth imbalance when concluding a real pan-retinal translational stress response.

The report failed to identify the data as single-nucleus RNA-seq despite the low mitochondrial content and nuclear_fraction column, inappropriately applying a 10% mitochondrial threshold instead of the 1-5% appropriate for nuclei.

It repeatedly quotes a 1.38-fold depth difference (from nFeature) when the actual per-cell count depth gap is ~1.6-fold, understating the confound it otherwise correctly flags, and the two 'robust' findings (MG gliosis, cone loss) are still asserted as robust despite resting on a single unreplicated library with that depth imbalance.

The report swaps the WT and DDX41 cell counts for several excluded cell types (e.g., Microglia, Endothelial) and confuses nFeature_RNA (median genes) with nCount_RNA (median transcripts) when calculating the depth difference.

The per-class cell counts given in the differential-expression section (e.g. rod 6,578 WT / 3,479 DDX41, cone 310/301, bipolar 1,197/1,312) contradict the composition table (rod 5,973/4,084, cone 499/112, BC 1,708/801), so the DE section's stated sample sizes are unsupported and appear fabricated or mislabelled.

The report fails to explicitly state the assumption that the data is single-nucleus (snRNA-seq) and adjust the mitochondrial QC threshold accordingly, despite the low median mitochondrial content and presence of a nuclear fraction column.

The per-class cell counts used for DE (e.g. Rod 6,578 WT / 3,479 DDX41; AC 469/181) contradict the dataset's own composition table (Rod 5,973/4,084; AC 258/392), and FDR-passing pathway counts are still reported as findings despite the stated pseudoreplication caveat.
The report hallucinates the per-arm cell counts for every major class in the Differential Expression section, completely contradicting the provided dataset tables.

The report never entertains that the pan-cell-type, same-direction up-shift in ribosomal/translation genes is a library-depth/normalisation artefact (DDX41 is ~1.6x deeper), instead building its central 'pan-retinal translational stress' claim on it — compounded by per-cell-type DE cell counts that contradict the composition table and FDR-based term counts reported as findings.

The report hallucinates incorrect cell counts per arm for every major class in the differential expression section and fails to recognize that the pan-retinal upregulation of ribosomal and translation genes is a classic artifact of the 1.6x sequencing depth difference between the two libraries.

Despite good depth/pseudoreplication caveats, it still reports FDR-based counts ('34 pathways at FDR<0.05') and NES/GSEA significance as findings, and the abstract/conclusion foreground rod phototransduction and 'metabolic reprogramming' as biology while the same depth artefact could inflate the mitochondrial/translation signal.
No major problems; the report excellently identifies both the lack of biological replication and the sequencing depth artifact driving the pan-cell-type shifts.

It still reports FDR<0.05 pathway counts per cell type as results and headlines an 'extreme' NES=-4.25 phototransduction finding, giving permutation-based statistics evidential weight the single-library design cannot support.
Reports FDR-thresholded pathway counts despite correctly acknowledging elsewhere that the lack of biological replicates makes p-values and FDRs invalid for inference.

Discussion cites specific genes and log2FCs (e.g. Gfap +6.02, Col25a1 +8.74, Grin2b/2d, C4b, A2m, Xlr3b) that never appear in the Results section, and GSEA is still run with an FDR 0.05 filter despite the stated pseudoreplication caveat.
No major problems; the report excellently identifies both the lack of biological replicates and the sequencing depth artefact driving the pan-retinal translation signal.
